entities.name: Robert of Bar, Count of Marle and Soissons
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Robert of Bar, born in 1390, was a prominent French noble whose brief but significant career was inextricably linked to the tumultuous Hundred Years' War and the internecine Armagnac-Burgundian civil strife. Holding the titles of Lord of Marle (1397–1413), Count of Marle (1413–1415), and Count of Soissons (1412–1415), Robert represented a generation of French aristocracy caught between loyalty to the Crown and the brutal realities of a fragmented kingdom. His lineage, a cadet branch of the House of Bar, positioned him as a key, albeit ultimately tragic, player in the early 15th-century French political landscape, embodying the martial ethos of the era.

His ascension to the County of Soissons in 1412, following the death of his cousin Louis of Bar, solidified his territorial influence in Picardy, a strategically vital region. Robert's military career reached its zenith, and its abrupt end, at the Battle of Agincourt on October 25, 1415. As a loyal supporter of the Armagnac faction and a direct vassal of the French Crown, he answered the call to arms against the invading forces of King Henry V of England. He fought valiantly alongside other high-ranking French nobles, including Duke Charles I of Orléans and Duke John I of Bourbon, in the ill-fated French vanguard.

Robert's death at Agincourt, at the age of 25, marked a significant blow to the French nobility, contributing to the staggering losses suffered by France. Without direct male heirs, his titles and lands, notably the County of Marle and Soissons, passed to his sister, Jeanne of Bar, who subsequently married Louis of Luxembourg, Count of Saint-Pol. This transfer of power further intertwined the destinies of powerful noble houses, shaping regional alliances and loyalties in the ongoing conflict and contributing to the gradual consolidation and fragmentation of feudal territories in northern France.
